docs.title: Implementation approach
docs.text:
Everything lives in one script, code/data.py, using NumPy, pandas, Matplotlib, scikit-learn (only PCA and OneHotEncoder) and SciPy's linprog (an exact feasibility check, not a model). It builds every dataset, saves Figures 1 to 7 to figures/ and writes every number quoted below to code/results.json. The Spaceship Titanic train.csv (8693 rows, the Kaggle file) is versioned in data/train.csv. The site's CI workflow runs this script before mkdocs gh-deploy, so the figures and results.json shown here are regenerated from the code on every deploy. To reproduce locally from the repository root:

pip install numpy pandas matplotlib scikit-learn scipy
python docs/exercises/data/code/data.py

Design choices:

  • One generator. rng = np.random.default_rng(42) is created once and used, in this order, for: the Exercise 1 noise, Dataset I, Dataset II, and the Exercise 3 train/test split. Nothing else draws random numbers. The split is implemented by hand with rng.permutation inside each class (instead of train_test_split(random_state=...)) so that the rule "same rng throughout" holds literally.
  • Same noise for every spread. In Exercise 1 the standard-normal noise Z (100 × 2 per class) is drawn once, and the dataset with spread s is mean + s · std · Z. The four datasets of item B therefore differ only in spread, and s = 1 is exactly the Figure 1 dataset.
  • Linear separability is tested, not guessed. The mixing rate uses the nearest-mean rule, which is only one particular set of straight boundaries. To answer "can the classes be separated by straight lines" I also solve a linear programme: does a linear layer with argmax (weights W, biases b) exist that puts every point in its own class with margin 1? Feasible means yes. Nothing is fitted to minimise an error, so no model is trained.
  • No leakage in Exercise 3. The split happens first; every median, mode, mean, std and the list of categories is computed on the training rows and then applied unchanged to the test rows.

Code (pulled from the file that was run):

"""
Data preparation and analysis -- Insper ANN-DL 2026.2, Exercise 1 (Data).

Run from the repository root:
    python docs/exercises/data/code/data.py

It builds every dataset, prints and saves every number the report quotes
(results.json), and saves Figures 1-7 to ../figures/.
A single generator, rng = np.random.default_rng(42), is used for everything
(Exercise 1 noise, Exercise 2 samples, the Exercise 3 split), so every run
produces exactly the same numbers and figures. No model is trained.
"""

import json
from itertools import combinations
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib

matplotlib.use("Agg")  # no display needed, we only save PNGs
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.optimize import linprog
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder

HERE = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
FIG_DIR = HERE.parent / "figures"
DATA_CSV = HERE.parent / "data" / "train.csv"
FIG_DIR.mkdir(exist_ok=True)

# The ONLY random generator in the whole script.
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)

R = {}  # every number quoted in the report ends up here -> results.json
COLORS = ["tab:blue", "tab:orange", "tab:green", "tab:red"]


def save(fig, name):
    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig(FIG_DIR / name, dpi=130)
    plt.close(fig)


# ===========================================================================
# Exercise 1 -- point clouds in 2D
# ===========================================================================
MEANS = np.array([[2, 3], [5, 6], [8, 1], [15, 4]], dtype=float)
STDS = np.array([[0.8, 2.5], [1.2, 1.9], [0.9, 0.9], [0.5, 2.0]])
N_PER_CLASS = 100
SCALES = [0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 4.0]

# A. Draw the standard-normal noise ONCE (100 x 2 per class). A dataset with
# spread s is mean + s * std * Z, so the four datasets of part B differ only
# in spread, not in which random points were drawn, and s = 1 is exactly the
# Figure 1 dataset.
Z = rng.standard_normal((4, N_PER_CLASS, 2))
y1 = np.repeat(np.arange(4), N_PER_CLASS)


def clouds(s):
    """400 x 2 points with all standard deviations multiplied by s."""
    return np.vstack([MEANS[k] + s * STDS[k] * Z[k] for k in range(4)])


X1 = clouds(1.0)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 5))
for k in range(4):
    ax.scatter(*X1[y1 == k].T, s=14, alpha=0.7, c=COLORS[k], label=f"Class {k}")
    ax.scatter(*MEANS[k], marker="X", s=180, c=COLORS[k], edgecolors="black")
ax.scatter([], [], marker="X", s=120, c="white", edgecolors="black", label="Class mean")
ax.set(title="Figure 1. Four Gaussian classes (s = 1)", xlabel="x1", ylabel="x2")
ax.legend()
save(fig, "fig1.png")

# Figure 1b (extra, item C.2): the boundaries an ideal classifier would draw,
# computed from the KNOWN generating Gaussians (Bayes rule, equal priors).
# Nothing is fitted; it is the target a trained network would approximate.
gx, gy = np.meshgrid(np.linspace(-3, 19, 500), np.linspace(-6, 12, 400))
G = np.c_[gx.ravel(), gy.ravel()]
loglik = np.stack([
    -np.sum(((G - MEANS[k]) / STDS[k]) ** 2, axis=1) / 2 - np.log(STDS[k]).sum()
    for k in range(4)
])
region = loglik.argmax(0).reshape(gx.shape)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 5))
ax.contourf(gx, gy, region, levels=[-0.5, 0.5, 1.5, 2.5, 3.5], colors=COLORS, alpha=0.15)
ax.contour(gx, gy, region, levels=[0.5, 1.5, 2.5], colors="black", linewidths=1)
for k in range(4):
    ax.scatter(*X1[y1 == k].T, s=12, alpha=0.7, c=COLORS[k], label=f"Class {k}")
ax.set(title="Figure 1b. Ideal (Bayes) decision regions from the true Gaussians",
       xlabel="x1", ylabel="x2")
ax.legend()
save(fig, "fig1b.png")

# B.1 Figure 2: four spreads, shared axis limits.
datasets = {s: clouds(s) for s in SCALES}
allpts = np.vstack(list(datasets.values()))
lims = (allpts.min(0) - 1, allpts.max(0) + 1)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(11, 8), sharex=True, sharey=True)
for ax, s in zip(axes.ravel(), SCALES):
    for k in range(4):
        ax.scatter(*datasets[s][y1 == k].T, s=8, alpha=0.6, c=COLORS[k], label=f"Class {k}")
    ax.set(title=f"s = {s}", xlabel="x1", ylabel="x2", xlim=(lims[0][0], lims[1][0]),
           ylim=(lims[0][1], lims[1][1]))
axes[0, 0].legend(fontsize=8)
fig.suptitle("Figure 2. Same means, standard deviations multiplied by s")
save(fig, "fig2.png")

# B.2 Separation ratio r_ij = ||mu_i - mu_j|| / (sbar_i + sbar_j), at s = 1.
sbar = STDS.mean(1)
pairs = []
for i, j in combinations(range(4), 2):
    dist = float(np.linalg.norm(MEANS[i] - MEANS[j]))
    r = dist / (sbar[i] + sbar[j])
    pairs.append({"pair": f"{i}-{j}", "dist": dist, "r_s1": r, "r_s2": r / 2})
smallest = min(pairs, key=lambda p: p["r_s1"])
R["ex1_sbar"] = sbar.tolist()
R["ex1_pairs"] = pairs
R["ex1_smallest_pair"] = smallest

# B.3 Mixing rate: fraction of points whose nearest TRUE class mean is not
# their own class mean.
def mixing_rate(X):
    d = np.linalg.norm(X[:, None, :] - MEANS[None, :, :], axis=2)
    return float((d.argmin(1) != y1).mean())

mix = {s: mixing_rate(datasets[s]) for s in SCALES}
R["ex1_mixing"] = {str(s): mix[s] for s in SCALES}
# per-pair confusion at each s (which classes get mixed)
conf = {}
for s in SCALES:
    d = np.linalg.norm(datasets[s][:, None, :] - MEANS[None], axis=2).argmin(1)
    conf[str(s)] = pd.crosstab(y1, d).reindex(index=range(4), columns=range(4), fill_value=0).values.tolist()
R["ex1_confusion_nearest_mean"] = conf

# Exact linear-separability check (no training): a linear programme asks
# whether weights W (4 x 2) and biases b (4) exist with
#   w_y . x + b_y >= w_k . x + b_k + 1   for every point x of class y, k != y.
# Feasible <=> a set of straight boundaries (a linear layer + argmax, i.e.
# convex polygonal regions) puts every point in its own class region.
def linearly_separable(X, y, n_cls):
    d = X.shape[1] + 1                    # weights + bias per class
    Xb = np.c_[X, np.ones(len(X))]
    rows = []
    for x, c in zip(Xb, y):
        for k in range(n_cls):
            if k == c:
                continue
            row = np.zeros(n_cls * d)
            row[c * d:(c + 1) * d] = -x   # -(w_c.x) + (w_k.x) <= -1
            row[k * d:(k + 1) * d] = x
            rows.append(row)
    res = linprog(np.zeros(n_cls * d), A_ub=np.array(rows), b_ub=-np.ones(len(rows)),
                  bounds=[(None, None)] * (n_cls * d), method="highs")
    return res.status == 0                # 0 = feasible, 2 = infeasible


def pairwise_separable(X):
    out = {}
    for i, j in combinations(range(4), 2):
        m = (y1 == i) | (y1 == j)
        out[f"{i}-{j}"] = linearly_separable(X[m], (y1[m] == j).astype(int), 2)
    return out


R["ex1_linsep_all4"] = {str(s): linearly_separable(datasets[s], y1, 4) for s in SCALES}
R["ex1_linsep_pairs"] = {str(s): pairwise_separable(datasets[s]) for s in SCALES}

# Figure 3 on a fine grid of s (same Z), so the onset of mixing is visible.
s_grid = np.round(np.arange(0.25, 4.01, 0.05), 2)
mix_grid = [mixing_rate(clouds(s)) for s in s_grid]
first_mix = float(s_grid[np.argmax(np.array(mix_grid) > 0)])
sep_grid = [linearly_separable(clouds(s), y1, 4) for s in s_grid]
last_sep = float(s_grid[np.flatnonzero(sep_grid).max()])
first_nonsep = float(s_grid[np.argmin(sep_grid)])
R["ex1_linsep_grid"] = {"last_separable_s": last_sep, "first_nonseparable_s": first_nonsep,
                        "monotone": bool(all(sep_grid[:np.argmin(sep_grid)]) and not any(sep_grid[np.argmin(sep_grid):]))}
R["ex1_smallest_r_at_first_nonsep"] = smallest["r_s1"] / first_nonsep
R["ex1_first_s_with_mixing"] = first_mix
R["ex1_smallest_r_at_first_mix"] = smallest["r_s1"] / first_mix
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4.5))
ax.plot(s_grid, mix_grid, c="gray", lw=1, label="fine grid of s")
ax.plot(SCALES, [mix[s] for s in SCALES], "o-", c="black", label="the 4 datasets")
ax.axvline(first_nonsep, ls="--", c="tab:red",
           label=f"no longer linearly separable, s = {first_nonsep}")
ax.set(title="Figure 3. Mixing rate vs. spread s", xlabel="s (std multiplier)",
       ylabel="mixing rate (nearest mean is wrong)")
ax.legend()
save(fig, "fig3.png")


# ===========================================================================
# Exercise 2 -- non-linearity in 5D
# ===========================================================================
N2 = 500
mu_A = np.zeros(5)
cov_A = np.array([
    [1.0, 0.8, 0.1, 0.0, 0.0],
    [0.8, 1.0, 0.3, 0.0, 0.0],
    [0.1, 0.3, 1.0, 0.5, 0.0],
    [0.0, 0.0, 0.5, 1.0, 0.2],
    [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.2, 1.0],
])
mu_B = np.full(5, 1.5)
cov_B = np.array([
    [1.5, -0.7, 0.2, 0.0, 0.0],
    [-0.7, 1.5, 0.4, 0.0, 0.0],
    [0.2, 0.4, 1.5, 0.6, 0.0],
    [0.0, 0.0, 0.6, 1.5, 0.3],
    [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.3, 1.5],
])
# Both matrices must be valid covariances (symmetric, positive definite).
R["ex2_min_eig"] = {"A": float(np.linalg.eigvalsh(cov_A).min()),
                    "B": float(np.linalg.eigvalsh(cov_B).min())}

# A. Dataset I
XA = rng.multivariate_normal(mu_A, cov_A, size=N2)
XB = rng.multivariate_normal(mu_B, cov_B, size=N2)
X_I = np.vstack([XA, XB])
y_I = np.repeat([0, 1], N2)


# B. Dataset II: random direction on the unit sphere times a random radius.
def shell(mean_radius, n=N2):
    v = rng.standard_normal((n, 5))
    u = v / np.linalg.norm(v, axis=1, keepdims=True)
    rho = rng.normal(mean_radius, 0.4, size=n)
    return rho[:, None] * u

XC = shell(2.0)
XD = shell(5.0)
X_II = np.vstack([XC, XD])
y_II = np.repeat([0, 1], N2)

# C.1 / C.2 PCA to 2D, one PCA per dataset (fitted on both classes together).
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 5))
for ax, (key, name, X, y, labels) in zip(axes, [
    ("I", "Dataset I (shifted Gaussians)", X_I, y_I, ["Class A", "Class B"]),
    ("II", "Dataset II (concentric shells)", X_II, y_II, ["Class C (core)", "Class D (shell)"]),
]):
    pca = PCA(n_components=2).fit(X)
    P = pca.transform(X)
    ev = pca.explained_variance_ratio_
    R[f"ex2_pca_{key}"] = {"pc1": float(ev[0]), "pc2": float(ev[1]), "sum": float(ev.sum())}
    R[f"ex2_pca_{key}"]["abs_cos_pc1_vs_ones"] = float(abs(pca.components_[0] @ (np.ones(5) / np.sqrt(5))))
    for c in (0, 1):
        ax.scatter(*P[y == c].T, s=8, alpha=0.6, c=COLORS[c], label=labels[c])
    ax.set(title=f"{name}\nPC1 {ev[0]:.1%}, PC2 {ev[1]:.1%}", xlabel="PC1", ylabel="PC2")
    ax.set_aspect("equal", adjustable="datalim")
    ax.legend()
fig.suptitle("Figure 4. PCA projections to 2D")
save(fig, "fig4.png")

# C.3 Distance between the (sample) class centers in 5D, and radius stats.
R["ex2_center_dist_I"] = float(np.linalg.norm(XA.mean(0) - XB.mean(0)))
R["ex2_center_dist_I_true"] = float(np.linalg.norm(mu_A - mu_B))
R["ex2_center_dist_II"] = float(np.linalg.norm(XC.mean(0) - XD.mean(0)))
norms = {k: np.linalg.norm(v, axis=1) for k, v in
         {"A": XA, "B": XB, "C": XC, "D": XD}.items()}
R["ex2_norm_stats"] = {k: {"mean": float(v.mean()), "min": float(v.min()), "max": float(v.max())}
                       for k, v in norms.items()}

# D.3 A simple separating function for Dataset II: f(x) = ||x||^2 - t.
# t is placed halfway (in radius) between the two mean radii: (2 + 5)/2 = 3.5.
t = 3.5 ** 2
pred_II = (np.sum(X_II ** 2, axis=1) > t).astype(int)
R["ex2_rule_threshold_sq"] = t
R["ex2_rule_accuracy"] = float((pred_II == y_II).mean())
R["ex2_gap"] = {"max_core_norm": float(norms["C"].max()), "min_shell_norm": float(norms["D"].min())}

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4.5))
bins = np.linspace(0, max(n.max() for n in norms.values()) + 0.5, 50)
for ax, (title, ks, labels) in zip(axes, [
    ("Dataset I", ["A", "B"], ["Class A", "Class B"]),
    ("Dataset II", ["C", "D"], ["Class C (core)", "Class D (shell)"]),
]):
    for c, (k, lab) in enumerate(zip(ks, labels)):
        ax.hist(norms[k], bins=bins, alpha=0.55, color=COLORS[c], label=lab)
    ax.set(title=title, xlabel="||x|| (5D Euclidean norm)", ylabel="count")
    ax.legend()
axes[1].axvline(3.5, ls="--", c="black", label="||x|| = 3.5")
axes[1].legend()
fig.suptitle("Figure 5. Distribution of ||x|| per class")
save(fig, "fig5.png")


# ===========================================================================
# Exercise 3 -- Spaceship Titanic
# ===========================================================================
SPEND = ["RoomService", "FoodCourt", "ShoppingMall", "Spa", "VRDeck"]
CAT_ONEHOT = ["HomePlanet", "CryoSleep", "Destination", "VIP"]

df = pd.read_csv(DATA_CSV)
R["ex3_shape_raw"] = list(df.shape)

# A.2 class balance
bal = df["Transported"].value_counts()
R["ex3_balance"] = {"True": int(bal[True]), "False": int(bal[False]),
                    "share_true": float(bal[True] / len(df))}

# A.4 missing-value table
miss = pd.DataFrame({"missing": df.isna().sum(), "pct": 100 * df.isna().mean()})
R["ex3_missing"] = {c: [int(r.missing), round(float(r.pct), 2)] for c, r in miss.iterrows()}
R["ex3_rows_with_any_nan"] = int(df.isna().any(axis=1).sum())

# A.5 spending stats (full raw file, NaN ignored)
R["ex3_spend_stats_full"] = {
    c: {"mean": float(df[c].mean()), "median": float(df[c].median()),
        "max": float(df[c].max()), "zero_share": float((df[c] == 0).mean())}
    for c in SPEND
}

# B. Stratified 80/20 split using the SAME rng: inside each class, permute
# the row indices and send the first 20% to test.
test_idx = []
for label in (False, True):
    idx = np.flatnonzero(df["Transported"].values == label)
    idx = rng.permutation(idx)
    test_idx.extend(idx[: int(round(0.2 * len(idx)))])
test_mask = np.zeros(len(df), dtype=bool)
test_mask[test_idx] = True
train, test = df[~test_mask].copy(), df[test_mask].copy()
R["ex3_split"] = {"train": len(train), "test": len(test),
                  "share_true_train": float(train["Transported"].mean()),
                  "share_true_test": float(test["Transported"].mean())}
R["ex3_foodcourt_train_raw"] = {"mean": float(train["FoodCourt"].mean()),
                                "median": float(train["FoodCourt"].median())}
foodcourt_raw_train = train["FoodCourt"].dropna().values  # for Figure 6
vrdeck_raw_train = train["VRDeck"].dropna().values          # for Figure 7

# C.1 Missing data. All statistics come from TRAIN only.
#  - spending: a CryoSleep passenger is confined to the cabin and spends 0
#    (checked below on train), so NaN -> 0 when CryoSleep is True; otherwise
#    NaN -> train median of that column.
#  - Age: train median (robust to the long right tail of ages).
#  - categorical: train mode.
R["ex3_cryo_spend_check_train"] = float(
    train.loc[train["CryoSleep"] == True, SPEND].fillna(0).sum(axis=1).max()
)
fit = {
    "age_median": float(train["Age"].median()),
    "spend_median": {c: float(train[c].median()) for c in SPEND},
    "mode": {c: train[c].mode()[0] for c in CAT_ONEHOT},
}


def impute(d):
    d = d.copy()
    for c in CAT_ONEHOT:
        d[c] = d[c].fillna(fit["mode"][c])
    asleep = d["CryoSleep"] == True
    for c in SPEND:
        d.loc[asleep & d[c].isna(), c] = 0.0
        d[c] = d[c].fillna(fit["spend_median"][c])
    d["Age"] = d["Age"].fillna(fit["age_median"])
    return d


train, test = impute(train), impute(test)
R["ex3_impute_fit"] = {"age_median": fit["age_median"], "spend_median": fit["spend_median"],
                       "mode": {k: str(v) for k, v in fit["mode"].items()}}

# C.3 Feature engineering (after imputation, so no NaN propagates).
for d in (train, test):
    d["TotalSpend"] = d[SPEND].sum(axis=1)
    d.drop(columns=["Cabin", "Name", "PassengerId"], inplace=True)

# C.2 One-hot encoding, fitted on train. handle_unknown="ignore": a category
# never seen in train becomes an all-zero row in that feature's block.
for d in (train, test):
    for c in CAT_ONEHOT:
        d[c] = d[c].astype(str)
enc = OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore", sparse_output=False).fit(train[CAT_ONEHOT])
onehot_names = list(enc.get_feature_names_out(CAT_ONEHOT))
demo = pd.DataFrame([{"HomePlanet": "Pluto", "CryoSleep": "False",
                      "Destination": "TRAPPIST-1e", "VIP": "False"}])
demo_row = enc.transform(demo)[0]
R["ex3_unknown_category_demo"] = {"input": demo.iloc[0].to_dict(),
                                  "HomePlanet_block": demo_row[:3].tolist()}

# C.4 Heavy tails: log(1 + x) on the five spending columns and TotalSpend.
LOG_COLS = SPEND + ["TotalSpend"]
for d in (train, test):
    d[LOG_COLS] = np.log1p(d[LOG_COLS])

# C.5 Standardization (z-score), mean and std from TRAIN only.
NUM = ["Age"] + LOG_COLS
mu, sd = train[NUM].mean(), train[NUM].std(ddof=0)


def build_matrix(d):
    num = ((d[NUM] - mu) / sd).values
    cat = enc.transform(d[CAT_ONEHOT])
    return np.hstack([num, cat])


Xtr, Xte = build_matrix(train), build_matrix(test)
ytr = train["Transported"].astype(int).values
yte = test["Transported"].astype(int).values
feature_names = NUM + onehot_names
R["ex3_features"] = feature_names
R["ex3_shape_train"] = list(Xtr.shape)
R["ex3_shape_test"] = list(Xte.shape)
R["ex3_nan_left"] = {"train": int(np.isnan(Xtr).sum()), "test": int(np.isnan(Xte).sum())}
R["ex3_range_numeric"] = {
    "train": [float(Xtr[:, : len(NUM)].min()), float(Xtr[:, : len(NUM)].max())],
    "test": [float(Xte[:, : len(NUM)].min()), float(Xte[:, : len(NUM)].max())],
}
R["ex3_range_full"] = {"train": [float(Xtr.min()), float(Xtr.max())],
                       "test": [float(Xte.min()), float(Xte.max())]}
R["ex3_per_column_range_train"] = {
    n: [round(float(Xtr[:, i].min()), 3), round(float(Xtr[:, i].max()), 3)]
    for i, n in enumerate(NUM)
}
R["ex3_train_mean_std_after"] = {
    n: [round(float(Xtr[:, i].mean()), 6), round(float(Xtr[:, i].std()), 6)]
    for i, n in enumerate(NUM)
}
# Share of |z| > 2 on the numeric block (where tanh starts to saturate).
R["ex3_share_abs_gt2_train"] = float((np.abs(Xtr[:, : len(NUM)]) > 2).mean())

# Figure 6: FoodCourt, raw train vs. final (log + z-score).
fc_final = Xtr[:, NUM.index("FoodCourt")]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4.5))
axes[0].hist(foodcourt_raw_train, bins=60, color="tab:blue", label="train, raw")
axes[0].set(title="Before: raw FoodCourt", xlabel="FoodCourt spend (credits)", ylabel="passengers")
axes[1].hist(fc_final, bins=60, color="tab:green", label="train, log1p + z-score")
axes[1].set(title="After: log(1+x), then standardized", xlabel="FoodCourt (z-score of log1p)",

docs.title: A. Generate the clouds
docs.text:
400 samples, 100 per class, each class an axis-aligned Gaussian:

Class Mean Std 0 [2, 3] [0.8, 2.5] 1 [5, 6] [1.2, 1.9] 2 [8, 1] [0.9, 0.9] 3 [15, 4] [0.5, 2.0]

Figure 1. Classes 0, 1 and 2 sit close together on the left and touch each other; class 3 is isolated on the right. The X markers are the class means.

docs.title: B. Spread
docs.text:
1. Four spreads. Same means and noise, all standard deviations multiplied by s ∈ {0.5, 1, 2, 4}.

Figure 2. Shared axis limits. At s = 0.5 the four clouds are compact and apart; at s = 4 classes 0, 1 and 2 are one blob and class 3 starts to merge with class 2.

2. Separation ratio at s = 1. r_ij = ‖μi − μj‖ / (σ̄i + σ̄j), with σ̄ = [1.65, 1.55, 0.90, 1.25] for classes 0 to 3.

Pair ‖μi − μj‖ r_ij (s = 1) r_ij (s = 2) 0-1 4.243 1.326 0.663 0-2 6.325 2.480 1.240 0-3 13.038 4.496 2.248 1-2 5.831 2.380 1.190 1-3 10.198 3.642 1.821 2-3 7.616 3.542 1.771

The smallest pair is 0-1 with r = 1.326. Multiplying every std by s multiplies every σ̄ by s and leaves the means unchanged, so r_ij(s) = r_ij(1) / s. At s = 2 it becomes 1.326 / 2 = 0.663: the distance between the two means is now smaller than the sum of their average spreads.

3. Mixing rate (share of points whose nearest true class mean is not their own):

s 0.5 1.0 2.0 4.0 Mixing rate 0.25% (1 point) 5.00% 20.25% 43.00% Linearly separable (all 4 classes)? yes no no no

At s = 1 the 20 mixed points are 8 of class 0 closer to μ1, 6 of class 1 closer to μ0 and 6 of class 1 closer to μ2. At s = 4 even class 3 loses 22 points (20 of them to class 2).

4. Figure 3.

Figure 3. Mixing rate vs. s. Black dots are the four datasets; the grey line repeats the computation for s from 0.25 to 4 in steps of 0.05 with the same noise. The red line marks where the linear programme becomes infeasible.

On the fine grid the classes are linearly separable up to s = 0.65 and not from s = 0.70 on (and never again for larger s). So the scale is s ≈ 0.7. There the smallest ratio is r_01 = 1.326 / 0.7 ≈ 1.89 (2.04 at s = 0.65): once the two closest means are less than about two "average spreads" apart, the tails of classes 0 and 1 cross and no straight line keeps them apart. The pair tests confirm it is 0-1 and 1-2 that break first.

Note that the nearest-mean rule already makes mistakes at s = 0.35, well before separability is lost (at s = 0.5 one point is "mixed" but a set of lines still separates everything). Class 0 is very elongated in x2 (std 2.5), so a point at the top of class 0 can be closer to μ1 than to μ0 while still being on the class-0 side of a well-placed line. The mixing rate is a measure of overlap, not a proof of non-separability.

docs.title: C. Analysis
docs.text:
1. Overlap at s = 1. Class 3 is far from everyone (r ≥ 3.5) and class 2 only touches class 1 at its upper-left edge. The real overlap is between classes 0 and 1 (r = 1.33): the top of class 0, which is stretched vertically, enters the bottom-left of class 1. The linear programme says the pairs 0-1 and 1-2 are not linearly separable at s = 1, while 0-2, 0-3, 1-3 and 2-3 are. One single linear boundary cannot separate four classes at all: a line only splits the plane in two half-planes, so at best it isolates one group (e.g. class 3 from the rest). A set of linear boundaries (three or more lines, or a linear layer with 4 outputs and argmax) gets almost everything right, but not 100% at s = 1: the few points of 0 and 1 that sit inside each other's cloud cannot be fixed by any straight boundary.

2. Sketch of the boundaries. Figure 1b draws the boundaries an ideal classifier would use, computed directly from the known generating Gaussians (Bayes rule, equal priors, nothing fitted). A trained network would learn something close to it:

Figure 1b. Ideal regions. A near-vertical, slightly curved line around x1 ≈ 3 to 6 between classes 0 and 1; a closed oval around class 2 (it is the tightest class, so its region is small and round); a vertical line near x1 ≈ 11.5 that cuts off class 3.

The boundaries are curved because the classes have different covariances (a quadratic discriminant). A small MLP with tanh units would approximate these curves with a few bent pieces; a purely linear model would replace them with straight segments and lose a few points near the 0-1 and 1-2 frontiers.

3. Relation to part B. The boundaries in Figure 1b depend only on the means and on the ratio between the class covariances, so they barely move when s grows. What grows is the share of each cloud that falls on the wrong side of them: the region where the network must make errors goes from a thin strip between classes 0 and 1 at s = 1 (5% mixing) to most of the left half of the plane at s = 4 (43%). No architecture can avoid those errors, because at that point the same (x1, x2) is genuinely produced by two different classes; more capacity would only fit noise.

docs.title: A. Dataset I (shifted Gaussians)
docs.text: Class A: 500 samples, mean 0, covariance Σ_A (positive correlation 0.8 between features 1 and 2). Class B: 500 samples, mean [1.5, …, 1.5], covariance Σ_B (larger variances, 1.5, and correlation −0.7 between features 1 and 2). Both matrices are valid covariances: their smallest eigenvalues are 0.158 and 0.498, both positive.

docs.title: B. Dataset II (concentric shells)
docs.text: 500 samples per class. Direction u = v / ‖v‖ with v ~ N(0, I₅) (uniform on the 5D unit sphere), radius ρ ~ N(2.0, 0.4) for the core (class C) and ρ ~ N(5.0, 0.4) for the shell (class D), point x = ρ · u.

docs.title: C. Visualize and compare
docs.text:
1. Figure 4.

Figure 4. PCA to 2D, one PCA per dataset fitted on both classes. Dataset I: the two classes are side by side along PC1, with a band of overlap. Dataset II: the core is a dense disk in the middle and the shell is spread around and over it.

2. Explained variance.

PC1 PC2 PC1 + PC2 Dataset I 51.0% 15.5% 66.4% Dataset II 21.7% 20.5% 42.1%

Dataset I's projection preserves the classification information much better. There the largest source of variance is the shift between the classes, so PC1 is almost the direction from μ_A to μ_B (|cos| = 0.99 with [1, 1, 1, 1, 1]/√5): the projection keeps exactly what separates them. Dataset II is spherically symmetric: every direction has the same variance (about 1/5 each, which is why PC1 and PC2 are both ≈ 21%), PCA has no preferred direction, and the useful information (the radius) is spread over all five coordinates. A 2D projection only sees part of ‖x‖, so shell points whose direction is mostly in the three discarded coordinates land in the middle, on top of the core.

3. In 5D.

  • Distance between the class centers (sample means): Dataset I: 3.356 (theory: ‖[1.5]·5‖ = 1.5√5 = 3.354). Dataset II: 0.261 (theory: 0, both shells are centered at the origin; 0.26 is sampling noise).

Figure 5. Histograms of ‖x‖ per class. Dataset I: the radii overlap a lot (A mean 2.13, B mean 4.22), because a shift is not a change in radius. Dataset II: two separate bumps; the largest core radius is 2.99 and the smallest shell radius is 3.85, so the dashed line ‖x‖ = 3.5 separates them with no error.

docs.title: D. Analysis
docs.text:
1. Same center, separate radii. A hyperplane w·x + b = 0 classifies a point by which side of it the point is on. Its decision depends on a linear projection w·x, and the average of w·x over a class is w·μ. When the two centers coincide, both classes have the same average on every hyperplane, and by symmetry each shell puts half of its points on each side of any hyperplane through the middle. The information that separates them, the distance to the origin, is not a direction in space, so no hyperplane captures it.

2. Why no linear boundary works, however much data. The core is a solid ball around the origin and the shell surrounds it in every direction. Take any hyperplane. If it passes through the ball, it also cuts the shell, with shell points on both sides. If it leaves the whole ball on one side, the shell still has points on that same side (the cap of the shell that faces the same way). So every half-space that contains the core also contains part of the shell. This is a property of the geometry, not of the sample: adding more data only fills the shell more densely and makes the contradiction certain. The best a hyperplane can do is cut off one cap of the shell and call everything else core, which leaves most of the shell misclassified; it can never reach the 100% of the radius rule below.

3. Does a mixed PCA plot prove inseparability? No. PCA is a linear projection that keeps the directions of largest variance, not the directions that separate classes, and it throws away 3 of the 5 dimensions. In Figure 4 Dataset II looks mixed, yet in 5D the classes are perfectly separable by a simple non-linear rule:

f(x) = ‖x‖² − 12.25 = x₁² + x₂² + x₃² + x₄² + x₅² − 3.5², predict shell if f(x) > 0.

This rule classifies all 1000 points correctly (100%), as Figure 5 already suggests. The threshold 3.5 is halfway between the two mean radii. Equivalently: adding the single feature ‖x‖² makes Dataset II linearly separable, which is exactly the kind of feature a hidden layer can learn.

docs.title: A. Get to know the data
docs.text:
1. Data. train.csv from the Kaggle Spaceship Titanic competition: 8693 rows, 14 columns.

2. Target. Transported says whether the passenger was transported to another dimension when the ship hit the spacetime anomaly (True/False). It is the label to predict. Balance: 4378 True (50.36%) and 4315 False (49.64%), practically balanced, so accuracy is a meaningful metric and no reweighting is needed.

3. Feature types.

  • Numerical: Age, RoomService, FoodCourt, ShoppingMall, Spa, VRDeck (the last five are credits spent on board).
  • Categorical: HomePlanet (Earth, Europa, Mars), CryoSleep (True/False), Destination (TRAPPIST-1e, 55 Cancri e, PSO J318.5-22), VIP (True/False), Cabin (deck/number/side string).
  • Identifiers / free text: PassengerId, Name.

4. Missing values.

Column Missing % PassengerId 0 0.00 HomePlanet 201 2.31 CryoSleep 217 2.50 Cabin 199 2.29 Destination 182 2.09 Age 179 2.06 VIP 203 2.34 RoomService 181 2.08 FoodCourt 183 2.11 ShoppingMall 208 2.39 Spa 183 2.11 VRDeck 188 2.16 Name 200 2.30 Transported 0 0.00

Each column only misses about 2%, but the gaps are spread over different rows: 2087 rows (24%) have at least one NaN, so dropping incomplete rows would throw away a quarter of the data.

5. Spending columns (full file, NaN ignored):

Column Mean Median Max Share of zeros RoomService 224.7 0 14 327 64.2% FoodCourt 458.1 0 29 813 62.8% ShoppingMall 173.7 0 23 492 64.3% Spa 311.1 0 22 408 61.2% VRDeck 304.9 0 24 133 63.2%

All medians are 0 while the means are in the hundreds and the maxima in the tens of thousands. Most passengers spend nothing, and a small group spends a lot: the mean is pulled up by the long right tail, so the distributions are extremely right-skewed (FoodCourt skewness on the training set: 6.6) and the spread is dominated by a few outliers. The median describes the typical passenger; the mean does not.

docs.title: B. Split before transforming
docs.text:
Stratified 80/20 split by Transported, done with the same rng: 6954 train / 1739 test rows, with 50.36% and 50.37% True respectively.

The test set must behave like data the model has never seen. If medians, means, stds or the category list are computed on the full file, information from the test rows enters the training features (data leakage) and the test score becomes optimistic. So the split comes first, and every statistic below is fitted on the 6954 training rows only and then applied to the test rows.

docs.title: C. Preprocess
docs.text:
1. Missing data (fitted on train, applied to test):

  • Categorical (HomePlanet, CryoSleep, Destination, VIP): training mode (Earth, False, TRAPPIST-1e, False). Each column misses only 2 to 2.5%, the mode is the most likely value, and it does not create an extra one-hot column.
  • Spending: if the passenger is in CryoSleep, the missing value is set to 0; I checked on the training set that the maximum total spend of CryoSleep passengers is exactly 0, so this is a fact, not a guess. Otherwise the training median, which is 0 for all five columns. The median (not the mean) is used because of the skew in A.5: the mean (≈ 450 for FoodCourt) would describe almost nobody.
  • Age: training median, 27. Robust to the right tail of ages (max 79).

2. One-hot encoding of HomePlanet, CryoSleep, Destination and VIP with scikit-learn's OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore"), fitted on train only. The encoder stores the categories it saw in train. A category that appears only in test (e.g. HomePlanet = "Pluto") does not raise an error and does not create a new column: its block of the row is all zeros (the script checks this and gets [0, 0, 0] for the HomePlanet block). The network then sees "none of the known planets", which is the honest input, and the matrix keeps the same 17 columns for train and test.

3. Feature engineering. TotalSpend = RoomService + FoodCourt + ShoppingMall + Spa + VRDeck (computed after imputation). Cabin, Name and PassengerId are dropped.

4. Heavy tails. log(1 + x) on the five spending columns and on TotalSpend. log(1 + 0) = 0, so the many zeros stay zeros, and a spend of 29 813 becomes 10.3.

Figure 7. VRDeck on the training set. Before: everything is squeezed into the first bar and the tail up to 24 133 is invisible. After: a spike at 0 (non-spenders) and a readable bump between about 1 and 9 (centred near 5.5) for the passengers who spend.

Why this helps a tanh network: tanh is only sensitive (non-saturated) for inputs roughly in [−2, 2]. Without the log, after scaling the few big spenders would have z-scores of 20 or more, pushing neurons into the flat part of tanh where the gradient is ≈ 0, and they would dominate the weight updates while the typical passenger is crushed near one value. The log compresses the tail (FoodCourt skewness goes from 6.6 to 1.1) so the scaled values stay in the useful range.

5. Scaling. Standardization (z-score) of the 7 numerical columns (Age + 5 spending + TotalSpend), with mean and std from train. I chose it over [−1, 1] min-max because min-max is set by the single largest value, which is still an outlier after the log, and because z-scores centre each feature at 0, where tanh has its maximum slope. After scaling, every numerical training column has mean 0.000 and std 1.000. One-hot columns stay 0/1.

  • Train: min −2.010, max 3.497.
  • Test: min −2.010, max 3.497.

Both extremes come from Age (ages 0 and 79 occur in both sets). Per column on train, the spending features range from about −0.66 to 3.28 and TotalSpend from −1.15 to 1.65.

docs.title: D. Verify and visualize
docs.text:
1. Figure 6.

Figure 6. FoodCourt on the training set, counts on a log axis in both panels. Before: raw credits from 0 to almost 30 000, monotonically decreasing tail. After log(1 + x) and z-score: values between −0.65 and 2.85; the non-spenders form the bar at −0.65 and the spenders a bump around 1 to 2.

2. Final checks.

  • NaN left: 0 in train and 0 in test.
  • Final shape: train 6954 × 17, test 1739 × 17 (7 numerical + 3 HomePlanet + 2 CryoSleep + 3 Destination + 2 VIP).
  • Range: every value is in [−2.01, 3.50]. Only 4.6% of the numerical training entries have |z| > 2. This suits tanh: the inputs are centred, of order 1, and few of them would push a unit with small initial weights into saturation.

3. Which decision matters most. The log transform of the spending columns is the one that most affects training. Five of the seven numerical features (plus TotalSpend) are spending, and without the log their standardized values would range from −0.3 to more than 20: a few rich passengers would saturate the tanh units and produce huge gradients, while the 63% who spend nothing and the moderate spenders would look almost identical. Imputation touches only about 2% of each column, and standardization alone cannot fix a skewed shape (it only shifts and rescales it), so the log is what turns these columns into inputs a tanh network can actually learn from.

# Exact linear-separability check (no training): a linear programme asks
# whether weights W (4 x 2) and biases b (4) exist with
#   w_y . x + b_y >= w_k . x + b_k + 1   for every point x of class y, k != y.
# Feasible <=> a set of straight boundaries (a linear layer + argmax, i.e.
# convex polygonal regions) puts every point in its own class region.
def linearly_separable(X, y, n_cls):
    d = X.shape[1] + 1                    # weights + bias per class
    Xb = np.c_[X, np.ones(len(X))]
    rows = []
    for x, c in zip(Xb, y):
        for k in range(n_cls):
            if k == c:
                continue
            row = np.zeros(n_cls * d)
            row[c * d:(c + 1) * d] = -x   # -(w_c.x) + (w_k.x) <= -1
            row[k * d:(k + 1) * d] = x
            rows.append(row)
    res = linprog(np.zeros(n_cls * d), A_ub=np.array(rows), b_ub=-np.ones(len(rows)),
                  bounds=[(None, None)] * (n_cls * d), method="highs")
    return res.status == 0                # 0 = feasible, 2 = infeasible

docs.title: Implementation approach
docs.text:
Everything lives in one script, code/mlp.py, with NumPy and Matplotlib. scikit-learn is used only where the statement allows it: make_blobs, make_classification, train_test_split, confusion_matrix and the two LogisticRegression baselines. The script saves Figures 1 to 6 to figures/ and writes every number quoted below to code/results.json. The site's CI workflow runs it before deploying and commits the figures and results.json back to the repository. To reproduce locally from the repository root:

pip install numpy matplotlib scikit-learn
python docs/exercises/mlp/code/mlp.py

Design choices:

  • One generator. rng = np.random.default_rng(42) is created once and used for every weight initialization and every mini-batch shuffle, in script order. The dataset functions and the split use random_state=42, as the statement prescribes.
  • One network class for everything. MLP(sizes, output, rng) takes the layer sizes as an argument (e.g. [2, 8, 1], [4, 32, 32, 3]). Hidden layers use tanh, and weights use Xavier/Glorot-normal initialization (std √(2 / (fan_in + fan_out)), suited to tanh) with zero biases. forward, backward and step are written once and reused unchanged in Exercises 2, 3 and 4 (see 3.B).
  • Mini-batch gradient descent, batch size 32, data reshuffled every epoch. The training loss recorded for the figures is the loss on the full training set at the end of each epoch.
  • Gradient check. At the end of the script, backward() is compared with central finite differences on a small random batch. The maximum relative error is 7.2 × 10⁻⁸ for sigmoid + BCE on [2, 8, 1] and 7.0 × 10⁻⁷ for softmax + CCE on [4, 32, 32, 3], so the hand-derived gradients are correct. This check runs after everything else, so it does not change the random stream used above.

Code (pulled from the file that was run):

"""
Multi-Layer Perceptron from scratch (NumPy) -- Insper ANN-DL 2026.2, MLP exercise.

Run from the repository root:
    python docs/exercises/mlp/code/mlp.py

It checks the Exercise 1 hand computation, builds the Exercise 2-4 datasets,
trains the MLPs, saves Figures 1-6 to ../figures/ and writes every number the
report quotes to results.json. One generator, rng = np.random.default_rng(42),
is used for every weight initialization and every mini-batch shuffle.
scikit-learn is only used for make_blobs, make_classification,
train_test_split, confusion_matrix and the LogisticRegression baselines.
"""

import json
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import matplotlib

matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.datasets import make_blobs, make_classification
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.metrics import confusion_matrix
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

HERE = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
FIG_DIR = HERE.parent / "figures"
FIG_DIR.mkdir(exist_ok=True)

# The ONLY random generator in the whole script.
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
R = {}


def save(fig, name):
    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig(FIG_DIR / name, dpi=130)
    plt.close(fig)


# ===========================================================================
# Exercise 1 -- numerical check of the hand computation (the report shows
# every step by hand; this only confirms the numbers).
# ===========================================================================
x = np.array([0.5, -0.2]); y = 1.0
W1 = np.array([[0.3, -0.1], [0.2, 0.4]]); b1 = np.array([0.1, -0.2])
W2 = np.array([0.5, -0.3]); b2 = 0.2; eta = 0.3

z1 = W1 @ x + b1
h1 = np.tanh(z1)
u2 = W2 @ h1 + b2
yhat = np.tanh(u2)
L = (y - yhat) ** 2
dL_dyhat = -2 * (y - yhat)
dL_du2 = dL_dyhat * (1 - yhat ** 2)
dL_dW2 = dL_du2 * h1
dL_db2 = dL_du2
dL_dh1 = dL_du2 * W2
dL_dz1 = dL_dh1 * (1 - h1 ** 2)
dL_dW1 = np.outer(dL_dz1, x)
dL_db1 = dL_dz1
W1n, b1n = W1 - eta * dL_dW1, b1 - eta * dL_db1
W2n, b2n = W2 - eta * dL_dW2, b2 - eta * dL_db2
L_after = (y - np.tanh(W2n @ np.tanh(W1n @ x + b1n) + b2n)) ** 2
R["ex1"] = {k: np.round(v, 6).tolist() for k, v in {
    "z1": z1, "h1": h1, "u2": u2, "yhat": yhat, "L": L, "dL_dyhat": dL_dyhat,
    "dL_du2": dL_du2, "dL_dW2": dL_dW2, "dL_db2": dL_db2, "dL_dh1": dL_dh1,
    "dL_dz1": dL_dz1, "dL_dW1": dL_dW1, "dL_db1": dL_db1, "W1_new": W1n,
    "b1_new": b1n, "W2_new": W2n, "b2_new": b2n, "L_after": L_after}.items()}


# ===========================================================================
# The MLP (shared by Exercises 2, 3 and 4)
# ===========================================================================
def sigmoid(u):
    return 1 / (1 + np.exp(-u))


def softmax(u):
    e = np.exp(u - u.max(axis=1, keepdims=True))  # shift for numerical stability
    return e / e.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)


def bce(P, Y):
    """Binary cross-entropy, mean over the batch. P, Y: (N, 1)."""
    P = np.clip(P, 1e-12, 1 - 1e-12)
    return float(-np.mean(Y * np.log(P) + (1 - Y) * np.log(1 - P)))


def cce(P, Y):
    """Categorical cross-entropy, mean over the batch. P, Y: (N, K), Y one-hot."""
    return float(-np.mean(np.sum(Y * np.log(np.clip(P, 1e-12, 1)), axis=1)))


class MLP:
    """Fully connected network: tanh hidden layers, sigmoid or softmax output.

    sizes  -- e.g. [2, 8, 1] or [4, 32, 32, 3] (input, hidden..., output)
    output -- "sigmoid" (pairs with BCE) or "softmax" (pairs with CCE)
    For both pairs the gradient of the loss w.r.t. the output pre-activation
    is (P - Y) / N, so backward() is identical for Exercises 2, 3 and 4.
    """

    def __init__(self, sizes, output, rng):
        self.sizes, self.out = sizes, {"sigmoid": sigmoid, "softmax": softmax}[output]
        # Xavier/Glorot-normal init (suited to tanh), zero biases
        self.W = [rng.normal(0, np.sqrt(2 / (a + b)), size=(a, b))
                  for a, b in zip(sizes[:-1], sizes[1:])]
        self.b = [np.zeros(b) for b in sizes[1:]]

    def n_params(self):
        return int(sum(W.size + b.size for W, b in zip(self.W, self.b)))

    def forward(self, X):
        """Returns output probabilities; stores every layer's activation."""
        self.A = [X]
        for l, (W, b) in enumerate(zip(self.W, self.b)):
            U = self.A[-1] @ W + b
            last = l == len(self.W) - 1
            self.A.append(self.out(U) if last else np.tanh(U))
        return self.A[-1]

    def backward(self, Y):
        """Gradients of the mean loss, by the chain rule, layer by layer."""
        N = len(Y)
        delta = (self.A[-1] - Y) / N              # dL/dU at the output layer
        self.gW, self.gb = [None] * len(self.W), [None] * len(self.W)
        for l in range(len(self.W) - 1, -1, -1):
            self.gW[l] = self.A[l].T @ delta       # dL/dW = a_prev^T delta
            self.gb[l] = delta.sum(axis=0)         # dL/db = sum of delta
            if l > 0:                              # through W, then tanh'
                delta = (delta @ self.W[l].T) * (1 - self.A[l] ** 2)

    def step(self, lr):
        for l in range(len(self.W)):
            self.W[l] -= lr * self.gW[l]
            self.b[l] -= lr * self.gb[l]


def train(model, X, Y, loss_fn, lr, epochs, batch, rng):
    """Mini-batch gradient descent; returns the full training loss per epoch."""
    history = []
    for _ in range(epochs):
        order = rng.permutation(len(X))
        for i in range(0, len(X), batch):
            idx = order[i:i + batch]
            model.forward(X[idx])
            model.backward(Y[idx])
            model.step(lr)
        history.append(loss_fn(model.forward(X), Y))
    return np.array(history)


def one_hot(y, k):
    return np.eye(k)[y]

# Exercise 2 -- binary, one class in the middle, the other on both sides

# Gradient check (done last so it does not change the rng stream above):
# compare backward() with central finite differences on a small batch.
def grad_check(sizes, output, loss_fn, k):
    m = MLP(sizes, output, rng)
    Xc = rng.normal(size=(5, sizes[0]))
    Yc = one_hot(rng.integers(0, k, 5), k) if output == "softmax" else rng.integers(0, 2, (5, 1)).astype(float)
    m.forward(Xc); m.backward(Yc)
    worst, eps = 0.0, 1e-6
    for P, G in list(zip(m.W, m.gW)) + list(zip(m.b, m.gb)):
        for idx in np.ndindex(P.shape):
            old = P[idx]
            P[idx] = old + eps; lp = loss_fn(m.forward(Xc), Yc)
            P[idx] = old - eps; lm = loss_fn(m.forward(Xc), Yc)
            P[idx] = old
            num = (lp - lm) / (2 * eps)
            worst = max(worst, abs(num - G[idx]) / max(1e-8, abs(num) + abs(G[idx])))
    return worst

R["grad_check_max_rel_error"] = {"sigmoid+BCE [2,8,1]": grad_check([2, 8, 1], "sigmoid", bce, 2),

Figure 1. Class 0 sits in the middle; class 1 is on both sides of it, along the diagonal.

docs.title: B. Baseline
docs.text: Logistic regression on the training set: test accuracy 47.5%, below chance. The fitted weights are almost zero (w = [0.030, 0.001], b = −0.003), so the model predicts ≈ 0.5 everywhere and its "boundary" (dashed line in Figure 3) is essentially arbitrary.

docs.title: C. MLP from scratch
docs.text:
• Architecture: 2 → 8 (tanh) → 1 (sigmoid), 33 parameters.
  • Loss: binary cross-entropy, L = −(1/N) Σ [y log p + (1 − y) log(1 − p)].
  • Backward: with a sigmoid output, ∂L/∂u = (p − y)/N at the output; then for each layer, going backwards: ∂L/∂W = aᵀδ, ∂L/∂b = Σδ, δ_prev = (δWᵀ) ⊙ (1 − a²) for the tanh layer below.
  • Training: learning rate 0.1, 500 epochs, batch size 32.
  • Test accuracy: 91.0% (train 96.5%). Training loss fell from 0.679 after epoch 1 to 0.104 after epoch 500.

Figure 2. Training BCE per epoch. Most of the drop happens in the first 50 epochs; after that the loss slowly flattens around 0.10.

Figure 3. Decision regions of the MLP over a grid (blue = class 0, orange = class 1), with the test points. The dashed line is the logistic-regression boundary.

docs.title: D. Analysis
docs.text:
Why the line fails. The two class-1 clusters are centered at (3, 3) and (−3, −3), so the mean of class 1 is (0, 0), exactly the mean of class 0. A straight line splits the plane into two half-planes. To get the center cluster right, the line must put (0, 0) on the class-0 side, but then at least one of the two outer clusters, which lie in opposite directions from the center, falls on the same side. Any line therefore gets about half of class 1 wrong, or cuts the center cluster in two. Logistic regression, which looks for one direction w where the classes differ on average, finds none (w ≈ 0 because the class means coincide). Its predictions are near 0.5 for every point, so the accuracy is set by noise and lands at 47.5%.

What the MLP builds. In Figure 3 the class-0 region is a band: a strip running from the upper left to the lower right, perpendicular to the diagonal on which the three clusters lie. Class 1 is the union of two separate regions, one on each side of the strip. That shape needs at least two boundaries: one on the (3, 3) side and one on the (−3, −3) side. Each hidden tanh unit is a soft step across its own line, and the output adds them up, so with two or more units the network can say "class 1 if beyond the upper boundary or beyond the lower one", which is exactly what this data requires. A single line can only make one half-plane, and a half-plane is convex. Here class 1 is not even connected (two pieces on opposite sides), so no half-plane can contain both pieces without also containing the strip between them. (The small blue patch at the top-left corner of the grid is an extrapolation artifact far from any data point.)

docs.text: make_classification with 1500 samples, 4 features (all informative), 3 classes, 2 clusters per class, class_sep=1.0, random_state=42. Split 80/20 stratified with random_state=42: 1200 train, 300 test (100 per class).

docs.title: B. Adaptation
docs.text:
The output layer has 3 units, softmax gives the probabilities, and the loss is categorical cross-entropy.

Derivation of ∂L/∂u for softmax + CCE. For one sample with logits u = (u₁, …, u_K), pₖ = e^{uₖ} / Σⱼ e^{uⱼ} and L = −Σₖ yₖ log pₖ, with y one-hot (Σₖ yₖ = 1).

  1. Softmax Jacobian: ∂pₖ/∂uᵢ = pₖ(δₖᵢ − pᵢ), where δₖᵢ = 1 if k = i, else 0.
  2. Chain rule: ∂L/∂uᵢ = −Σₖ (yₖ / pₖ) · ∂pₖ/∂uᵢ = −Σₖ yₖ (δₖᵢ − pᵢ) = −yᵢ + pᵢ Σₖ yₖ.
  3. Since Σₖ yₖ = 1: ∂L/∂uᵢ = pᵢ − yᵢ. Averaged over a batch of N samples: ∂L/∂U = (P − Y)/N.

This is the same form as sigmoid + BCE in Exercise 2, where ∂L/∂u = (p − y)/N. That is why backward() starts from delta = (A[-1] - Y) / N and serves both cases.

Extra point: code reused unchanged. Exercises 2, 3 and 4 call the same MLP.forward, MLP.backward, MLP.step and train functions, with no edits and no if on the task. What changes: the sizes ([2, 8, 1] → [4, 32, 3] → [4, 32, 32, 3]), the loss (bce → cce), the output nonlinearity that goes with that loss ("sigmoid" → "softmax", passed as an argument), and the hyperparameters. The output nonlinearity is part of the loss choice: sigmoid + BCE is the two-class special case of softmax + CCE, which is why both give the same output gradient.

docs.title: C. Training and evaluation
docs.text:
• Architecture: 4 → 32 (tanh) → 3 (softmax), 259 parameters.
  • Hyperparameters: learning rate 0.05, 300 epochs, batch size 32.
  • Test accuracy: 84.3% (253 of 300). Final training loss 0.248.

Figure 4. Training CCE per epoch, from 0.77 to 0.25; still decreasing slowly at epoch 300.

Figure 5. Test confusion matrix (rows = true class, columns = predicted). Diagonal: 86, 79, 88.

docs.title: D. Analysis
docs.text:
Most-confused pair: classes 0 and 1, with 19 test errors between them (12 class-1 points predicted as 0, 7 class-0 points predicted as 1). Next is 1 ↔ 2 (15 errors), then 0 ↔ 2 (13). Class 1 is the hardest class overall (79/100 correct).

Why, from the cluster structure. make_classification places 6 Gaussian clusters (2 per class) at vertices of a hypercube in the 4 informative dimensions, with side 2 · class_sep = 2; which vertices each class gets is random. So each class is two blobs that can be far from each other, and the class regions are not convex: a class-0 blob can sit right next to a class-1 blob, closer than the other class-0 blob is. With class_sep=1.0, neighbouring vertices are only 2 units apart while each cluster has a spread of roughly 1 unit per dimension, so neighbouring blobs overlap in their tails. The confusion concentrates on the pair of classes whose blobs happen to be neighbours on the cube, here 0 and 1. Those points are genuinely ambiguous, so no classifier gets them all right.

Baseline: logistic regression gets 66.3% on the same split. Its errors are mostly between classes 1 and 2 (57 test errors: 32 + 25). A linear softmax model gives each class one convex region (an intersection of half-spaces). Here each class has two separate blobs, so one convex region either misses one of the blobs or swallows the blob of another class lying between them. The hidden layer adds the missing ingredient: the 32 tanh units build features (soft half-space indicators) in which each class can be the union of separate regions. The output layer then recombines them, so each class can own both of its blobs. That alone is worth +18 points of accuracy (66.3% → 84.3%), and the confusion moves from "structurally impossible" errors (1 ↔ 2) to the real tail overlaps between neighbouring blobs.

docs.title: A. Training
docs.text:
Same data, split, learning rate (0.05), epochs (300), batch size (32), activation and initialization as Exercise 3; only the depth changes.

  • Architecture: 4 → 32 (tanh) → 32 (tanh) → 3 (softmax), 1315 parameters.
  • Test accuracy: 85.7% (257 of 300) in the run shown in Figure 6. Final training loss 0.186.

docs.title: B. Comparison
docs.text:
Figure 6. Training loss of the two networks, same axes. The 2-hidden-layer network drops faster and ends lower (0.186 vs 0.248), with more epoch-to-epoch jitter.

Five runs per model (≥ 3 seeds). Each run draws its own initialization and shuffles from the shared rng, so the runs differ only in their position in the random stream:

hidden layers parameters final train loss (mean of 5) test accuracy (mean ± std of 5) Exercise 3 1 259 0.247 84.5% ± 0.6 Exercise 4 2 1315 0.180 85.5% ± 0.6

Per run, test accuracy: 1 hidden layer 85.3, 84.3, 85.0, 83.7, 84.0%; 2 hidden layers 85.0, 86.0, 84.7, 85.7, 86.3%. Mean difference: +1.07 percentage points for the deeper network. Mean training accuracy: 91.2% (1 hidden) vs 93.6% (2 hidden).

docs.title: C. Analysis
docs.text:
Result. Here the deeper network is slightly better, +1.1 points on average. That is not much more than the spread between runs (std 0.6 points, and the run ranges overlap), and it is about 3 extra test points out of 300. So the honest reading is "a small, plausible gain", not "depth clearly helps".

What the data needs. The task has 6 clusters in 4D, and the ideal boundaries between neighbouring Gaussian blobs are smooth, close to piecewise-linear surfaces. One hidden layer of 32 tanh units can already carve the space into regions that cover all 6 blobs; that is what took the accuracy from 66% to 84%. The remaining errors come from overlapping tails, which no boundary can fix. A second layer can compose features (regions built from regions), but this problem has little hierarchical structure to exploit, so there is little left for it to add.

What depth costs. The second layer brings 5× the parameters (1315 vs 259) and a longer chain of tanh derivatives for the gradient to pass through. Here the depth is small and the Xavier initialization keeps the signal healthy, so optimization did not get harder: the loss actually fell faster per epoch (Figure 6). The cost shows elsewhere: the noisier loss curve, and capacity that goes into memorizing the training set.

Do training loss and test accuracy agree? Only partly. Training loss falls by 27% (0.247 → 0.180) and training accuracy rises 2.4 points, but test accuracy rises only 1.1 points; the train-test gap grows from 6.7 to 8.0 points. Most of what the extra layer gains on the training set is fitting noise in the overlapping tails, and it does not transfer. A lower training loss is not evidence of a better model here.

What data would reward depth. Data with compositional, hierarchical structure, where useful features are built from simpler features: images (edges → textures → parts → objects), audio, text, or tabular problems with strong multiplicative interactions between many variables (e.g. parity-like or XOR-of-many-features rules). There, a deep network represents the target with far fewer units than a shallow one would need. A few overlapping Gaussian blobs is about the opposite case.

class MLP:
    """Fully connected network: tanh hidden layers, sigmoid or softmax output.

    sizes  -- e.g. [2, 8, 1] or [4, 32, 32, 3] (input, hidden..., output)
    output -- "sigmoid" (pairs with BCE) or "softmax" (pairs with CCE)
    For both pairs the gradient of the loss w.r.t. the output pre-activation
    is (P - Y) / N, so backward() is identical for Exercises 2, 3 and 4.
    """

    def __init__(self, sizes, output, rng):
        self.sizes, self.out = sizes, {"sigmoid": sigmoid, "softmax": softmax}[output]
        # Xavier/Glorot-normal init (suited to tanh), zero biases
        self.W = [rng.normal(0, np.sqrt(2 / (a + b)), size=(a, b))
                  for a, b in zip(sizes[:-1], sizes[1:])]
        self.b = [np.zeros(b) for b in sizes[1:]]

    def n_params(self):
        return int(sum(W.size + b.size for W, b in zip(self.W, self.b)))

    def forward(self, X):
        """Returns output probabilities; stores every layer's activation."""
        self.A = [X]
        for l, (W, b) in enumerate(zip(self.W, self.b)):
            U = self.A[-1] @ W + b
            last = l == len(self.W) - 1
            self.A.append(self.out(U) if last else np.tanh(U))
        return self.A[-1]

    def backward(self, Y):
        """Gradients of the mean loss, by the chain rule, layer by layer."""
        N = len(Y)
        delta = (self.A[-1] - Y) / N              # dL/dU at the output layer
        self.gW, self.gb = [None] * len(self.W), [None] * len(self.W)
        for l in range(len(self.W) - 1, -1, -1):
            self.gW[l] = self.A[l].T @ delta       # dL/dW = a_prev^T delta
            self.gb[l] = delta.sum(axis=0)         # dL/db = sum of delta
            if l > 0:                              # through W, then tanh'
                delta = (delta @ self.W[l].T) * (1 - self.A[l] ** 2)

    def step(self, lr):
        for l in range(len(self.W)):
            self.W[l] -= lr * self.gW[l]
            self.b[l] -= lr * self.gb[l]

def train(model, X, Y, loss_fn, lr, epochs, batch, rng):
    """Mini-batch gradient descent; returns the full training loss per epoch."""
    history = []
    for _ in range(epochs):
        order = rng.permutation(len(X))
        for i in range(0, len(X), batch):
            idx = order[i:i + batch]
            model.forward(X[idx])
            model.backward(Y[idx])
            model.step(lr)
        history.append(loss_fn(model.forward(X), Y))
    return np.array(history)

docs.title: Implementation approach
docs.text:
Everything lives in one script, code/perceptron.py, written with NumPy and Matplotlib only. It generates both datasets, trains the perceptron, saves Figures 1 to 6 to figures/, and writes every number quoted below to code/results.json. To reproduce from the repository root:

pip install -r requirements.txt
python docs/exercises/perceptron/code/perceptron.py

Design choices:

  • One generator. rng = np.random.default_rng(42) is created once at the top and used, in this order, for: Exercise 1 data, the Exercise 1 initial weights, Exercise 2 data, the Exercise 2 initial weights. Nothing else draws random numbers, so the numbers below are identical on every run.
  • Shuffling. After the 1000 + 1000 points are drawn, the rows are permuted once (with the same rng). Without this the online loop would see all of Class 0 and then all of Class 1, which only changes the order of updates, but makes the run depend on an arbitrary stacking order.
  • One training function. train_perceptron implements the activation, the prediction, the {0,1} error-driven rule and the stopping condition. Exercise 2 calls the same function unchanged; the pocket bookkeeping (a full-dataset accuracy check after each update, and a copy of (w, b) when it improves) is inside it and is harmless on separable data, where the pocket simply ends equal to the final weights.
  • Same initialization for the η = 1.0 re-run. w is drawn once from rng.normal(0, 0.01, size=2) and the same vector is passed to both Exercise 1 runs, so η is really the only thing that changes.

Challenges: the pocket check evaluates the whole dataset after every update (about 78 000 updates in Exercise 2), which is the slowest part, but the script still runs in about 10 s. Figure 3 includes an epoch-0 point (accuracy of the initial weights) because Exercise 1 converges so fast that a curve starting at epoch 1 would be flat.

Code (pulled from the file that was run):

"""
Perceptron from scratch (NumPy only) -- Insper ANN-DL 2026.2, Exercise 2.

Run from the repository root:
    python docs/exercises/perceptron/code/perceptron.py

It generates both datasets, trains the perceptron, prints every number the
report quotes, saves Figures 1-6 to ../figures/ and writes results.json.
A single generator, rng = np.random.default_rng(42), is used for everything,
so every run produces exactly the same numbers and figures.
"""

import json
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import matplotlib

matplotlib.use("Agg")  # no display needed, we only save PNGs
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

HERE = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
FIG_DIR = HERE.parent / "figures"
FIG_DIR.mkdir(exist_ok=True)

# The ONLY random generator in the whole script.
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)

ETA = 0.01          # learning rate from the statement
MAX_EPOCHS = 100    # epoch cap from the statement
N_PER_CLASS = 1000  # samples per class


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Data generation
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
def make_dataset(mean0, cov0, mean1, cov1, n=N_PER_CLASS):
    """Draw n points per class from two 2D Gaussians and shuffle them.

    Class 0 gets label 0 and class 1 gets label 1. The rows are shuffled once
    (with the same rng) so the training loop does not see all class-0 points
    first and then all class-1 points.
    """
    x0 = rng.multivariate_normal(mean0, cov0, size=n)
    x1 = rng.multivariate_normal(mean1, cov1, size=n)
    X = np.vstack([x0, x1])
    y = np.concatenate([np.zeros(n, dtype=int), np.ones(n, dtype=int)])
    order = rng.permutation(len(y))
    return X[order], y[order]


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The perceptron (activation, prediction, update rule, training loop)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
def step(z):
    """Heaviside activation: 1 if z >= 0, else 0."""
    return (z >= 0).astype(int)


def predict(X, w, b):
    """y_hat = step(w . x + b) for every row of X."""
    return step(X @ w + b)


def accuracy(X, y, w, b):
    """Fraction of points of the full dataset classified correctly."""
    return float(np.mean(predict(X, w, b) == y))


def train_perceptron(X, y, w0, b0=0.0, eta=ETA, max_epochs=MAX_EPOCHS):
    """Online perceptron with the {0,1} error-driven rule and a pocket.

    For each sample (x, y):
        y_hat = step(w . x + b)
        w <- w + eta * (y - y_hat) * x
        b <- b + eta * (y - y_hat)
    (y - y_hat) is 0 on a correct prediction, so only mistakes update.

    Stops after an epoch with zero updates, or after max_epochs.

    Pocket: after every update the accuracy on the full dataset is computed;
    if it beats the best seen so far, (w, b) is copied into the pocket.
    On separable data the pocket simply ends equal to the final weights.
    """
    w = np.array(w0, dtype=float).copy()
    b = float(b0)

    # Pocket starts with the initial weights.
    pocket_w, pocket_b = w.copy(), b
    pocket_acc = accuracy(X, y, w, b)
    pocket_epoch = 0

    history = {"acc": [], "pocket_acc": [], "updates": []}
    converged = False

    for epoch in range(1, max_epochs + 1):
        n_updates = 0
        for xi, yi in zip(X, y):
            y_hat = 1 if (xi @ w + b) >= 0 else 0  # same rule as step()
            error = yi - y_hat                    # 0, +1 or -1
            if error != 0:
                w += eta * error * xi
                b += eta * error
                n_updates += 1
                # Pocket bookkeeping: the only addition to the loop.
                acc_now = accuracy(X, y, w, b)
                if acc_now > pocket_acc:
                    pocket_w, pocket_b = w.copy(), b
                    pocket_acc = acc_now
                    pocket_epoch = epoch

        history["acc"].append(accuracy(X, y, w, b))
        history["pocket_acc"].append(pocket_acc)
        history["updates"].append(n_updates)

        if n_updates == 0:  # a full clean pass: converged
            converged = True
            break

    return {
        "w": w, "b": b, "acc": accuracy(X, y, w, b),
        "epochs": epoch, "converged": converged,
        "pocket_w": pocket_w, "pocket_b": pocket_b,
        "pocket_acc": pocket_acc, "pocket_epoch": pocket_epoch,
        "history": history,
    }


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Plotting helpers (every plot: title, axis labels, class legend)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
COLORS = {0: "#1f77b4", 1: "#ff7f0e"}


def scatter_classes(ax, X, y):
    for c in (0, 1):
        m = y == c
        ax.scatter(X[m, 0], X[m, 1], s=8, alpha=0.5, c=COLORS[c],
                   label=f"Class {c}")
    ax.set_xlabel("$x_1$")
    ax.set_ylabel("$x_2$")


def draw_boundary(ax, w, b, X, **kw):
    """Draw w1*x1 + w2*x2 + b = 0 across the x-range of the data."""
    x1 = np.linspace(X[:, 0].min() - 1, X[:, 0].max() + 1, 200)
    if abs(w[1]) > 1e-12:
        ax.plot(x1, -(w[0] * x1 + b) / w[1], **kw)
    else:  # vertical line
        ax.axvline(-b / w[0], **kw)


def mark_errors(ax, X, y, w, b, marker="x", color="red", label="Misclassified"):
    wrong = predict(X, w, b) != y
    if wrong.any():
        ax.scatter(X[wrong, 0], X[wrong, 1], marker=marker, s=30,
                   c=color, linewidths=1, label=f"{label} ({wrong.sum()})")
    return int(wrong.sum())


def save(fig, name):
    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig(FIG_DIR / name, dpi=150)
    plt.close(fig)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Exercise 1 -- separable data
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
X1, y1 = make_dataset([1.5, 1.5], [[0.5, 0], [0, 0.5]],
                      [5.0, 5.0], [[0.5, 0], [0, 0.5]])

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 5))
scatter_classes(ax, X1, y1)
ax.set_title("Figure 1 - Exercise 1: separable data (2000 points)")
ax.legend()
save(fig, "fig1.png")

# Initialization: w ~ N(0, 0.01), b = 0. Drawn ONCE and reused for the
# eta = 1.0 re-run, so that eta is the only thing that changes.
w_init_1 = rng.normal(0, 0.01, size=2)

r1 = train_perceptron(X1, y1, w_init_1, eta=0.01)
r1_eta1 = train_perceptron(X1, y1, w_init_1, eta=1.0)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 5))
scatter_classes(ax, X1, y1)
draw_boundary(ax, r1["w"], r1["b"], X1, color="black", lw=2,
              label="Decision boundary ($\\eta$=0.01)")
n_err_1 = mark_errors(ax, X1, y1, r1["w"], r1["b"])
ax.set_ylim(X1[:, 1].min() - 1, X1[:, 1].max() + 1)
ax.set_title("Figure 2 - Exercise 1: learned decision boundary")
ax.legend(loc="upper left")
save(fig, "fig2.png")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4))
# epoch 0 = accuracy of the initial weights, before any training
acc0_1 = accuracy(X1, y1, w_init_1, 0.0)
ax.plot(np.arange(0, r1["epochs"] + 1), [acc0_1] + r1["history"]["acc"],
        "o-", label="$\\eta$ = 0.01")
ax.plot(np.arange(0, r1_eta1["epochs"] + 1), [acc0_1] + r1_eta1["history"]["acc"],
        "s--", label="$\\eta$ = 1.0 (item D)")
ax.set_xticks(np.arange(0, max(r1["epochs"], r1_eta1["epochs"]) + 1))
ax.set_xlabel("Epoch")
ax.set_ylabel("Accuracy on the full dataset")
ax.set_title("Figure 3 - Exercise 1: accuracy x epoch")
ax.legend()
ax.grid(alpha=0.3)
save(fig, "fig3.png")


def unit(v):
    return v / np.linalg.norm(v)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Exercise 2 -- overlapping data
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
X2, y2 = make_dataset([3.0, 3.0], [[1.5, 0], [0, 1.5]],
                      [4.0, 4.0], [[1.5, 0], [0, 1.5]])

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 5))
scatter_classes(ax, X2, y2)
ax.set_title("Figure 4 - Exercise 2: overlapping data (2000 points)")
ax.legend()
save(fig, "fig4.png")

w_init_2 = rng.normal(0, 0.01, size=2)
r2 = train_perceptron(X2, y2, w_init_2, eta=ETA)  # same function, unchanged

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 5.5))
scatter_classes(ax, X2, y2)
draw_boundary(ax, r2["w"], r2["b"], X2, color="red", lw=2, ls="--",
              label="Final boundary")
draw_boundary(ax, r2["pocket_w"], r2["pocket_b"], X2, color="black", lw=2,
              label="Pocket boundary")
mark_errors(ax, X2, y2, r2["pocket_w"], r2["pocket_b"], marker="x",
            color="black", label="Misclassified by pocket")
mark_errors(ax, X2, y2, r2["w"], r2["b"], marker="o", color="none",
            label="Misclassified by final")
# hollow red circles for the final-weight errors
for coll in ax.collections[-1:]:
    coll.set_edgecolor("red")
    coll.set_facecolor("none")
ax.set_xlim(X2[:, 0].min() - 0.5, X2[:, 0].max() + 0.5)
ax.set_ylim(X2[:, 1].min() - 0.5, X2[:, 1].max() + 0.5)
ax.set_title("Figure 5 - Exercise 2: final vs pocket boundary")
ax.legend(loc="upper left", fontsize=8)
save(fig, "fig5.png")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))
ep2 = np.arange(1, r2["epochs"] + 1)
ax.plot(ep2, r2["history"]["acc"], lw=1, label="Current weights")
ax.plot(ep2, r2["history"]["pocket_acc"], lw=2, label="Pocket (best so far)")
ax.axhline(0.5, color="gray", ls=":", label="Chance (50%)")
ax.set_xlabel("Epoch")
ax.set_ylabel("Accuracy on the full dataset")
ax.set_title("Figure 6 - Exercise 2: accuracy x epoch")
ax.legend()
ax.grid(alpha=0.3)
save(fig, "fig6.png")

# Where does the final boundary cut the diagonal x1 = x2 = t ?
# (w1 + w2) t + b = 0  ->  t = -b / (w1 + w2)
t_final = -r2["b"] / r2["w"].sum()
t_pocket = -r2["pocket_b"] / r2["pocket_w"].sum()
pred_final = predict(X2, r2["w"], r2["b"])

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Supplementary checks quoted in the D items (they draw nothing from rng)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Ex1 D3: from a zero start, eta only rescales the weights.
z_a = train_perceptron(X1, y1, np.zeros(2), eta=0.01)
z_b = train_perceptron(X1, y1, np.zeros(2), eta=1.0)
zero_start = {
    "epochs_eta001": z_a["epochs"], "epochs_eta1": z_b["epochs"],
    "w_ratio": (z_b["w"] / z_a["w"]).tolist(),
    "b_ratio": z_b["b"] / z_a["b"],
}

# Ex2 D1: best accuracy any straight line reaches on THIS sample.
# Sweep directions theta and, for each, every threshold along the projection.
best_line_acc = 0.0
for theta in np.linspace(0, np.pi, 721):
    d = np.array([np.cos(theta), np.sin(theta)])
    proj = X2 @ d
    order = np.argsort(proj)
    ys = y2[order]
    # predict 1 to the right of the cut: correct = (#0 left) + (#1 right)
    zeros_left = np.concatenate([[0], np.cumsum(ys == 0)])
    ones_right = np.concatenate([[0], np.cumsum((ys == 1)[::-1])])[::-1]
    best_line_acc = max(best_line_acc, ((zeros_left + ones_right).max()) / len(ys))

# Ex2 D3: more epochs / smaller eta (same data, same initial weights).

docs.title: A — Generate the data
docs.text:
Class 0: mean [1.5, 1.5], covariance [[0.5, 0], [0, 0.5]]. Class 1: mean [5, 5], covariance [[0.5, 0], [0, 0.5]]. 1000 samples per class (function make_dataset).

Figure 1. The two classes are far apart relative to their spread: there is a wide empty corridor between them.

docs.title: B — Implement the perceptron
docs.text:
• Prediction: ŷ = step(w·x + b), with step(z) = 1 if z ≥ 0 and 0 otherwise (step, predict).
  • Update, for each sample: w ← w + η(y − ŷ)x and b ← b + η(y − ŷ). The error y − ŷ is 0 on a correct prediction, +1 on a false negative and −1 on a false positive, so both kinds of mistake get corrected.
  • Initialization: w = [0.00991, −0.00827] (drawn from rng.normal(0, 0.01, size=2)), b = 0.
  • η = 0.01; stop after an epoch with zero updates or after 100 epochs; accuracy on the full dataset recorded after every epoch.

docs.title: C — Train and measure
docs.text:
• Final w = [0.03189, 0.02874], final b = −0.200.
  • Epochs: 2. Epoch 1 made 48 updates; epoch 2 made 0 updates, which is the stopping condition.
  • Final accuracy: 100.0% (0 misclassified points). The initial weights scored 61.5%.

The boundary 0.03189·x₁ + 0.02874·x₂ − 0.200 = 0 crosses the diagonal x₁ = x₂ at 3.30, inside the empty corridor between the two means (1.5 and 5).

Figure 2. Decision boundary over the data. No point is misclassified, so there are no markers.

Figure 3. Accuracy × epoch (epoch 0 = initial weights). Both learning rates reach 100% at the end of epoch 1 and stop at epoch 2.

docs.title: D — Analysis
docs.text:
1. Why separable data converges quickly. An update happens only when y − ŷ ≠ 0, i.e. only on a mistake. Each mistake pushes w toward the misclassified point (+x for a false negative, −x for a false positive), so the boundary moves to the correct side of it. Because a separating line exists with a large margin, the number of points the current line gets wrong can only shrink: here it went from 48 updates in epoch 1 to 0 in epoch 2. Once a full pass has no mistakes, nothing in the rule can change w or b anymore, so training stops by itself.

2. η = 1.0. Same data, same initial w, only η changed:

Run Epochs Updates (epoch 1) Accuracy w b w / ‖w‖ η = 0.01 2 48 100% [0.03189, 0.02874] −0.20 [0.7429, 0.6694] η = 1.0 2 25 100% [1.71734, 1.66459] −11.0 [0.7181, 0.6960]

The two directions differ by 2.09°, and the boundaries cross the diagonal at 3.30 and 3.25: both separate the data perfectly, but they are different lines. Writing the weights after the training as w = w₀ + η Σ eᵢxᵢ (eᵢ = ±1 on the mistakes), dividing by η gives w/η = w₀/η + Σ eᵢxᵢ. The boundary only depends on w up to scale, so what matters is how big the initial vector is compared with one update. With ‖w₀‖ ≈ 0.013: for η = 0.01 the initial term w₀/η has norm ≈ 1.3, comparable to a single data point (‖x‖ between 2 and 7), so the random start still shapes which points are misclassified and in what order. For η = 1.0 the initial term is ≈ 0.013, negligible after the very first update, so the run behaves almost like a zero start. η therefore controls the relative weight of the initialization against each correction: it changes the sequence of mistakes (48 vs 25) and hence which of the many separating lines is found, not whether one is found.

3. Zero start. Let w₀ = 0, b₀ = 0 and compare two runs with η₁ and η₂ on the same data in the same order. Claim: after every step k, w_k^(2) = (η₂/η₁) w_k^(1) and b_k^(2) = (η₂/η₁) b_k^(1).

  • Step 0: both are 0, so the claim holds.
  • Inductive step: if the claim holds at step k, then for the next sample w^(2)·x + b^(2) = (η₂/η₁)(w^(1)·x + b^(1)). Since η₂/η₁ > 0, multiplying by it does not change the sign, so step(·) gives the same ŷ in both runs and the same error e = y − ŷ. The updates are η₁e·x and η₂e·x = (η₂/η₁)·η₁e·x, so after the update the claim still holds.

So both runs make exactly the same mistakes, at the same samples, in the same epochs: same epoch count, and the weights differ only by the factor η₂/η₁. The boundary {w·x + b = 0} is unchanged by scaling (w, b) by a positive constant, so η has no effect at all. Running it confirms this: from zero, η = 0.01 and η = 1.0 both stop at epoch 2, and the ratios of w₁, w₂ and b between the runs are all exactly 100.0. This is why item B forbids the zero start: with it, the η comparison in item 2 would be empty.

The pocket best was found during epoch 40. For reference, the best accuracy any straight line reaches on this particular sample (exhaustive sweep over directions and offsets, in the script) is 70.75%, so the pocket is essentially optimal for this draw. The ~73% in the statement is what the best line reaches in expectation; with the theoretical distributions the Bayes-optimal line x₁ + x₂ = 7 gives Φ(0.577) ≈ 72%, and a finite sample of 2000 points lands a little above or below that.

The final iterate did not drop all the way to 50% in this run; it ends at 64.85% and its per-epoch accuracy wanders between 60.8% and 68.3% (Figure 6). Item D explains why it sits below the pocket and why its value is essentially arbitrary.
